transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-08-25
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Jared Lewis (Head of Search, TideFinder), Priya Malhotra (ML Engineer), Sam Ortega (CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be short):
- Intro + high-level hosted API walkthrough (embeddings endpoint, rerank endpoint)
- Discussed similarity metrics, normalization, top_k and MMR knobs, and cost/latency tradeoffs for TideFinder's query patterns
- Agreed next steps: pilot pricing, sample eval, and a 6-week onboarding plan

Topics: Hosted embeddings, Rerank endpoint, Top-K, MMR, normalization, latency SLOs, SOC2/security, pilot plan

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Ethan (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Ethan Park, account exec for Redwood Inference. With me is Maya, our solutions engineer. How's it going over there?
[00:12] Jared (TideFinder): Good, thanks. Hi Ethan, hi Maya. We're excited to see the hosted flow. We run a pretty heavy product search and similarity stack, lots of short queries during peak.
[00:21] Maya (Redwood): Great, thanks Jared. We'll walk through the Hosted API for embeddings and then demo the rerank endpoint and Console/Optimize quick wins. We'll also talk about knobs for cost vs latency.
[00:33] Sam (TideFinder): Quick thing on our side — we prefer hosted if the SLA makes sense and data residency isn't an issue. If not, we'll consider private with VPC.
[00:41] Priya (TideFinder): Also, our query distribution skews lots of short queries with occasional bulk reindexing jobs. Latency target is sub-120ms p50 for interactive search if possible.
[00:52] Maya (Redwood): Good to know. A couple quick qualification points: do you batch queries client-side at all, or is it one-by-one? And what's your current similarity metric — dot product, cosine?
[01:05] Jared (TideFinder): One-by-one mostly. We use cosine similarity on embeddings from an in-house encoder. We do occasional MMR post-filtering.

[01:18] Maya (Redwood): Ok. On the hosted embeddings endpoint we support configurable vector norms and an option to return pre-normalized embeddings to match your cosine pipeline. For rerank we offer a dedicated /rerank endpoint that consumes candidate IDs plus query embedding and returns a scored ordering — supports MMR-style diversity and also ranker models if you want learned re-ranking.

[01:42] Jared: So the rerank service — does it do on-the-fly embedding computation or do we pass embeddings?
[01:47] Maya: You can do either. For minimal latency we often recommend computing embeddings client-side or in your ingest pipeline and passing stored vectors; the rerank endpoint accepts both raw text or embeddings. If you pass embeddings, we skip the encoder and reduce latency.

[02:05] Sam: What's the delta in latency between passing embeddings vs raw text? Rough numbers?
[02:10] Maya: For hosted on our standard tier, passing embeddings into rerank typically adds ~15-30ms vs a few hundred ms if we encode text server-side, depending on sequence length. Those are ballparks — we'll share bench notes.

[02:28] Ethan: To align on cost tradeoffs: embedding compute in the pipeline vs at inference changes the per-query cost. If you precompute and store, storage + retrieval cost vs compute per call — Redwood Optimize provides suggestions for quantization and batching to reduce cost.

[02:45] [00:03 silence, typing]

[03:00] Maya: Demo time. I'll share my screen — pulling up the Console. (screen noise) The Console shows per-route latency, token breakdown, and a rerank playground where you paste candidates and test scoring policies.
[03:22] Maya: Here we have a sample index of news articles. I run a query, we fetch top 100 candidates from your vector DB (we often integrate with Pinecone/Weaviate/your DB), then call Redwood's /rerank with the top 10 and get back reordered results with scores.

[03:45] Maya: Note — when we talk about top_k for search we mean the candidate pool size we send to rerank. Sending 100 -> rerank top 10 gives better recall but increased cost and some latency. For many apps, top_k=50 works well.

[04:05] Priya: We noticed in previous tests that normalizing embeddings on ingestion vs at query time changed recall a bit. Does Redwood normalize for cosine under the hood?
[04:14] Maya: We can do both. The hosted embeddings endpoint can return L2-normalized vectors (so cosine is dot product). If you store normalized vectors, rerank assumes dot-product; if not, you can pass an explicit flag. There are edge cases with mixed vector sources where it's safer to do normalization in a consistent pipeline.

[04:33] [04:33 Jared interrupts] Jared: I want to ask about batching — our traffic is spiky, with short bursts. Can Redwood autoscale?
[04:40] Ethan: For hosted, we autoscale with capacity pools and provide latency SLOs per tier. For peak bursts, we suggest brief bursts to dedicated or reserved capacity and fallback policies. Redwood's smart routing can route to alternate model variants to keep the app online.

[04:58] Maya: Also, Optimize will suggest batch window settings — it can automatically pick small batching delays that reduce cost by improving throughput while keeping p95 latency within your SLO. It's workload-aware.

[05:12] Sam: Security wise, what's the data flow? We have PII.
[05:16] Maya: On hosted, data is encrypted in transit and at rest. We offer SOC2 Type II, SSO/SAML for console access, and customer-controlled KMS is available on private deployments. For hosted we also have audit logs retained depending on plan. We'll send the security pack.

[05:34] Jared: Do you store queries or embeddings? Our policy is to not store raw user queries beyond transient logs.
[05:40] Ethan: By default, hosted stores minimal logs; customers can opt-out of retention or choose private deployment. We'll include details in the security doc.

[05:53] [05:53 Maya screen demo — typing]

[06:10] Maya: Back to the rerank API: you'll see a parameter like "diversity: m" for MMR-style scoring and "score_model: linear" for linear combination of signals. You can surface metadata signals too — freshness, popularity — and our rerank supports mixing learned and heuristic scores.

[06:33] Priya: For our use case, we want to apply a recency boost and also penalize stale docs. Is that configurable at request time?
[06:40] Maya: Yes, you send metadata along with candidate list and pass a small config block that weights recency. The config is JSON-ish in the request. (note: some transcription systems show the payload badly)

[06:55] Jared: About model choices — can we select smaller encoders for low latency?
[07:00] Maya: Yup — Hosted API has a model catalog. You can pick compact embedding models that trade a bit of semantic fidelity for speed and cost. Optimize can recommend which model for your traffic profile.

[07:18] [07:18 Jared asks] Jared: If we want deterministic rerank across regions, do you support model pinning?
[07:24] Maya: Yes, you can pin model versions per route. For stricter guarantees, Redwood Dedicated or Private allows deployment to a specific region and control plane.

[07:37] Sam: Any mention of quotas and burst limits we should be aware of?
[07:42] Ethan: Hosted tier has soft quotas; we can set custom quotas and alerts. For production scale, committed capacity is recommended. We'll map that against your expected QPS.

[07:56] Maya: Now I'll do a quick end-to-end with a small prompt set — pulling a short query log from our sample. (demo) Sending query, fetching candidates from our mock DB, calling /rerank with 20 candidates and a recency weight. You can see timing: 48ms for fetch + 22ms rerank = ~70ms total in this lab environment. Your production latency may vary.

[08:23] Priya: Those timings look optimistic for our infra but helpful. Can you share the benchmarking kit?
[08:29] Maya: Yes — I'll attach the bench harness and a tiny script you can run locally. We'll also provide a spreadsheet mapping cost per 1M queries with typical top_k settings.

[08:41] [08:41 brief cross talk, background noise]

[09:00] Jared: On accuracy — how do you measure rerank quality? Do you support running evals in Console?
[09:06] Maya: Console has a simple eval runner. You upload labeled query->relevant doc sets and run A/B between model+config pairs. Optimize can auto-suggest parameter sweeps (top_k, diversity, normalization) and show precision@k and MRR changes.

[09:25] Priya: We have a 1,000-query benchmark. Would Redwood run a pilot evaluation?
[09:30] Ethan: Yes, that's part of the pilot. Maya will run the sandbox evaluation and share results. For confidentiality we'll use your sample data behind a secure workspace.

[09:44] Maya: Quick note on vector storage: if you use an external vector DB, Redwood integrates via connectors. For lower cost you can use Redwood's integrated vector store — it's optimized for prefix cache and hot shards for low-latency reads. There's a tradeoff in control vs convenience.

[10:05] Jared: Which vector DBs do you integrate with?
[10:08] Maya: Pinecone, Weaviate, Opensearch's vector nodes, Milvus, and generic S3-backed stores with Redwood indexing. We'll share integration docs.

[10:20] Sam: Anything about cold-cache penalties for re-ranking at scale?
[10:24] Maya: Cold KV caches can add 10s-100s ms on first hot path. For typical search with moderate QPS, caching + prefetch reduces that. Optimize suggests pre-warming tactics for expected query sets.

[10:40] [10:40 Maya toggles to Optimize tab]

[10:53] Maya: Here in Optimize you can run a quantization suggestion — e.g., 8-bit quantization for the encoder reduced compute by ~2.5x in our internal tests with small quality delta for retrieval tasks. For rerank models we often keep them higher fidelity.

[11:11] Priya: We care about reproducibility. If we quantize, will results shift a lot?
[11:16] Maya: There will be small numeric shifts. Optimize runs A/B style evals so you can quantify the delta for your prompt set. It's best practice to guardrail quality with eval thresholds before fully rolling out.

[11:33] Jared: Ok — let's talk concrete pilot. Our success criteria: 1) maintain or improve precision@10 by at least 3% over baseline, 2) p50 latency under 120ms, 3) predictable cost within a 20% deviation of your estimate. Timeline: 6–8 weeks.

[11:52] Ethan: That's doable. We'll propose a 6-week pilot: week 1 onboarding & infra mapping, weeks 2–3 integration + bench, weeks 4–5 tuning + eval, week 6 rollout plan and handover.

[12:08] Priya: For billing — do you charge per embedding request, per rerank call, or per token?
[12:14] Ethan: Embeddings and rerank calls have unit pricing: embeddings per vector, rerank per candidate processed + base call. We'll send an example invoice projecting cost at your QPS and top_k. Also options for committed discounts if you pick reserved capacity.

[12:32] [12:32 short pause]

[12:45] Maya: A few technical gotchas we often see: mixed normalization between stored vectors and incoming embeddings, inconsistent dimension sizes from different encoders, and forgetting to pass metadata with timestamps for recency. Those cause subtle rank regressions.

[13:03] Jared: On the dimension point — we use a 768-d encoder but our historic embeddings are 512. Can Redwood handle mixing?
[13:10] Maya: Technically you must use consistent dims for dot-product pipelines. If you have mixed dims, we recommend re-encoding the legacy vectors or using a cross-encoder style reranker that takes raw text candidates and query text, but that's slower. We'll scope options in the pilot.

[13:30] Priya: Is there an option to do a hybrid: candidate retrieval with approximate vectors then a small cross-encoder for final scoring?
[13:36] Maya: Yes; our rerank endpoint supports passing in a small cross-encoder model for final score. It's a two-step pattern: fast vector recall + slow cross-encoder for top N. Works well when you need precision over latency for top results.

[13:55] Sam: About observability — can we see token-level cost per route and traces?
[13:59] Maya: Console shows per-route cost and latency breakdown, traces for individual requests, and you can hook into our tracing API. We also produce per-token cost estimates in the Optimize tab.

[14:17] Jared: Any concerns around vendor lock-in?
[14:21] Ethan: The API is fairly standard, and we support exporting model outputs and vectors. For private deployments you get more portability. We try to make migrations feasible but cross-team work is always needed.

[14:36] Priya: Do you run any QA on model updates? We want to avoid silent regressions when you change a model backend.
[14:42] Maya: We do Redwood-verified profiles and we recommend pinning model versions. Console has eval gating — you can auto-block rollouts if precision drops. We'll show the audit trail in the security pack.

[15:00] Jared: Ok great. Can you also run an end-to-end synthetic load test against our staging?
[15:06] Ethan: Yes — part of the pilot we do a staged load test. We'll need VPN or staged credentials; Priya can share details.

[15:15] Priya: I'll provision a staging endpoint and a dataset extract. Also, what's the recommended candidate pool size for our product search?
[15:22] Maya: It depends on catalog size — for thousands of items top_k 50–100 is common. For catalogs <50k, top_k 50 usually works. Optimize can sweep it.

[15:37] [15:37 background murmur]

[15:50] Ethan: Quick commercial note: we have a standard hosted agreement with SOC2; if you need a tighter contract or IP terms, we can escalate to legal.

[16:00] Sam: We will want an SLA and some data residency notes.

[16:04] Ethan: Understood. We'll include SLA options and private deployment pricing as an appendix.

[16:12] Maya: I'll drop links in the follow-up: bench harness repo, security pack, integration docs, and a sample rerank prompt set.

[16:21] Jared: Nice. One more technical question — can rerank incorporate click signals or telemetry as features?

[16:27] Maya: Yep, you can pass that as metadata; if you use a learned reranker we can ingest those as features during training or online learning. We'll discuss offline vs online approaches in the pilot.

[16:40] Priya: About training — do you support incremental training of rerankers in your platform or do we bring our own models?

[16:46] Maya: Both. For faster iteration you can use our hosted ranker templates where we do parameter tuning; for full control you bring your own model artifact and we can host it in the Dedicated/Private environments.

[17:00] Ethan: Time check — we're getting toward the end; want to recap next steps.

[17:05] Maya: Recap: 1) Maya will run the sandbox eval on your 1k queries and share the results; 2) Ethan will send pilot pricing + 6-week plan; 3) Priya will provide sample embeddings and a staging endpoint.

[17:18] Jared: Sounds good. Also please include the cost estimate for top_k 50 and 100 and an option with committed reserved capacity.

[17:26] Ethan: Will do. Anything else?

[17:30] Sam: No, thanks — appreciate the walkthrough.

[17:33] Ethan: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email with the docs.

[17:40] [Call ends, informal chatter fades]

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-hears: "KV cache" transcribed as "K V cash" in one snippet; small punctuation issues; timestamps approximate.
